Write each ball's height as a function of **one common clock** and set them equal.
**Step 1 — start the clock when the first ball is thrown.** With u = 39·2 m s⁻¹ and
g = 9·8 m s⁻²:
h₁ = 39·2t − 4·9t²
**Step 2 — write the second ball, thrown 2 s later.** At time t it has been in the air
for (t − 2) seconds:
h₂ = 39·2(t − 2) − 4·9(t − 2)²
**Step 3 — set them equal, since they meet.**
39·2t − 4·9t² = 39·2t − 78·4 − 4·9(t² − 4t + 4)
**Step 4 — expand and cancel.** The 39·2t and the 4·9t² terms cancel from both sides:
0 = −78·4 + 19·6t − 19·6
19·6t = 98
**t = 5 s**
**Step 5 — find the height.**
h = 39·2(5) − 4·9(25)
= 196 − 122·5
= **73·5 m** ✓
**Where each ball is at that moment.**
ball 1, 5 s after launch: it reached the top at 39·2/9·8 = 4 s, so it is **falling**
ball 2, 3 s after launch: still **rising**, since its peak comes at 4 s ✓
They meet with the first coming down and the second going up - the usual picture for
this type of problem.
**A check on ball 2.**
h₂ = 39·2(3) − 4·9(9) = 117·6 − 44·1 = **73·5 m** ✓ the same height, as required.
**A quicker route — relative motion.** In the frame of ball 1, ball 2 has **no
acceleration**, since gravity acts equally on both ✓ At the instant ball 2 is launched,
ball 1 is at 39·2(2) − 4·9(4) = **58·8 m** with velocity 39·2 − 19·6 = **19·6 m s⁻¹**
upward. Ball 2 approaches it at 39·2 − 19·6 = **19·6 m s⁻¹**, closing 58·8 m in
58·8/19·6 = **3 s** ✓ the same meeting time.
**Reading the distractors.** **196·0 m** ✗ is close to the maximum height of either ball
(78·4 m) multiplied up - no ball ever reaches 196 m here, since u²/2g = **78·4 m** is the
ceiling ✓ That single bound rules out both 117·6 m and 196·0 m immediately. **44·1 m** ✗
is the height at t = 1·5 s or thereabouts, not the meeting point.
∴ 73·5 m.

The same meeting problem, with rounder numbers: write both heights on one clock and
equate.
**Step 1 — first ball.** With u = 45 m s⁻¹ and g = 10 m s⁻², measuring t from its launch:
h₁ = 45t − 5t²
**Step 2 — second ball, launched 2 s later.**
h₂ = 45(t − 2) − 5(t − 2)²
**Step 3 — equate.**
45t − 5t² = 45t − 90 − 5(t² − 4t + 4)
45t − 5t² = 45t − 90 − 5t² + 20t − 20
**Step 4 — cancel and solve.** The 45t and 5t² terms cancel:
0 = −110 + 20t
**t = 5·5 s**
**Step 5 — find the height.**
h = 45(5·5) − 5(5·5)²
= 247·5 − 151·25
= **96·25 m** ✓
**Checking with the second ball.** It has been flying for 3·5 s:
h₂ = 45(3·5) − 5(3·5)²
= 157·5 − 61·25
= **96·25 m** ✓ identical, confirming the meeting.
**Which way each is moving.** Both balls peak 4·5 s after their own launch, so at the
meeting
ball 1, at 5·5 s, is **descending**
ball 2, at 3·5 s, is still **ascending** ✓
**The relative-motion check.** When ball 2 is launched, ball 1 is at
45(2) − 5(4) = **70 m** moving up at 45 − 20 = **25 m s⁻¹**. Ball 2 rises at 45 m s⁻¹, so
it gains at 45 − 25 = **20 m s⁻¹** - constant, because gravity cancels between them ✓
Closing 70 m at 20 m s⁻¹ takes **3·5 s**, matching exactly.
**The ceiling that bounds the answer.** Neither ball can exceed
u²/2g = 2025/20 = **101·25 m** ✓ so 162·7 m and 217·0 m are impossible on sight, and the
answer must be just below the peak - which 96·25 m is.

Both cars cover the **same distance** from rest, so relate their times through that
distance and then compare the finishing speeds.
**Step 1 — name the times.** Let car B take T and car A take T − t, both starting from
rest over the same distance s:
s = ½a₁(T − t)² = ½a₂T²
**Step 2 — take square roots.** All quantities are positive:
√a₁ (T − t) = √a₂ T
so
**T − t = T√(a₂/a₁)**
**Step 3 — solve for T.**
t = T[1 − √(a₂/a₁)]
= T(√a₁ − √a₂)/√a₁
so
**T = t√a₁/(√a₁ − √a₂)**
**Step 4 — write the two finishing speeds.** From rest, v = at:
v_A = a₁(T − t) = a₁T√(a₂/a₁) = T√(a₁a₂)
v_B = a₂T
**Step 5 — subtract.**
v = v_A − v_B
= T[√(a₁a₂) − a₂]
= T√a₂(√a₁ − √a₂)
**Step 6 — substitute T.**
v = [t√a₁/(√a₁ − √a₂)] x √a₂(√a₁ − √a₂)
= **t√(a₁a₂)** ✓
the (√a₁ − √a₂) factors cancelling exactly.
**A numerical check.** Take a₁ = 4, a₂ = 1 m s⁻² and s = 50 m:
car A: T_A = √(2 x 50/4) = **5 s**, finishing at v = 4(5) = **20 m s⁻¹**
car B: T_B = √(100) = **10 s**, finishing at v = 1(10) = **10 m s⁻¹**
so t = 10 − 5 = **5 s** and v = 20 − 10 = **10 m s⁻¹**
and the formula gives t√(a₁a₂) = 5√4 = **10 m s⁻¹** ✓ exact.
**Testing the distractors on the same numbers.** With t = 5, a₁ = 4, a₂ = 1:
2a₁a₂t/(a₁ + a₂) = 40/5 = **8** ✗
√(2a₁a₂) t = √8 x 5 = **14·1** ✗
(a₁ + a₂)t/2 = **12·5** ✗
Only √(a₁a₂) t gives 10 ✓ A single worked case separates all four options.
**Why the geometric mean appears.** Distances from rest go as **at²**, so equal distances
force a **square-root** relation between the accelerations ✓ Square roots multiplied
together give the geometric mean √(a₁a₂), not the arithmetic or harmonic one.
∴ v = √(a₁a₂) t.

Both trains decelerate, so each has only **half** the gap in which to stop.
**Step 1 — see how the 2 km is shared.** The two trains approach each other and brake
identically, so by symmetry each covers the same distance before stopping. To **barely**
avoid collision they must come to rest just as they meet, each having travelled
s = 2000/2 = **1000 m** ✓
**Step 2 — apply v² = u² + 2as to one train.** It goes from 40 m s⁻¹ to rest:
0 = 40² − 2a(1000)
2000a = 1600
**a = 0·8 m s⁻²** ✓
**The relative-motion route, which avoids the halving.** In the frame of one train, the
other approaches at 80 m s⁻¹ with a relative deceleration of 2a, and must stop within the
full 2000 m:
0 = 80² − 2(2a)(2000)
8000a = 6400
**a = 0·8 m s⁻²** ✓ the same answer, and a useful check that the "half the gap" step was
right.
**How long the stop takes.**
t = u/a = 40/0·8 = **50 s** ✓ a long, gentle braking - which is realistic for trains, and
is why signalling distances are so great.
**Is 0·8 m s⁻² achievable?** It is about **8% of g**, a mild deceleration comparable to
ordinary service braking ✓ The much larger options would be violent: 11 m s⁻² exceeds g
itself and would throw passengers forward harder than free fall.
**Why "barely avoid" matters.** It sets the **minimum** deceleration ✓ Any larger value
stops the trains sooner and leaves a gap; any smaller and they collide. The equality is
what makes the problem determinate.
**Reading the distractors.** **2·1 m s⁻²** ✗ would stop each train in 381 m, well short -
safe, but not the **minimum** asked for. **11·0** and **11·8 m s⁻²** ✗ are larger still,
and physically implausible for a train ✓
**A useful check on the arithmetic.** Stopping distance = u²/2a = 1600/1·6 = **1000 m** ✓
exactly half the gap, as required.
∴ 0·8 m/s².
